title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
authors: William Fedus, Barret Zoph, Noam Shazeer

pages.title: Scale by adding experts, not by making each token do more work

blocks.html: Dense Transformers scale by making every parameter participate in every forward pass — bigger model means more FLOPs per token. That cost is the wall.

Mixture of Experts (MoE) breaks the link: each token is routed to only a small subset of the model's parameters (the 'experts'). The model can have 10× the parameters of a dense baseline while costing roughly the same per-token FLOPs to train and run.

Switch Transformer simplifies the standard MoE recipe by routing each token to exactly one expert (k=1, instead of the k=2 that prior work used). This 'switch' routing is simpler, faster, and — surprisingly — works at least as well as top-2.

Switch Transformer achieves a 4-7× speedup over a strongly tuned T5-Base and a 4× speedup over T5-Large with the same computational resources. We further demonstrate that large sparse models trained with low precision (bfloat16) reach quality comparable to high precision dense models trained for much longer.

pages.title: Replacing the FFN with a Switch FFN

blocks.html: Take a standard Transformer. Inside each block there's a feed-forward network (FFN) that all tokens pass through. The Switch Transformer replaces this single FFN with $N$ independent FFNs (the experts) plus a small router.

For each token's hidden state $x$, the router computes $h = W_r x$ (a learned linear projection) and applies softmax to produce scores over experts. With top-1 routing, the token is sent to the highest-scoring expert $i^*$:
Only one expert runs per token. The expert's output is scaled by the router probability (so gradients flow back to the router). All other experts contribute nothing for that token.
Routing is learned — but you don't want all tokens to pile onto one or two experts. That defeats the parallelism: idle experts waste capacity, hot experts bottleneck.
An auxiliary load-balancing loss is added during training. It pushes the routing to distribute tokens uniformly across experts:
$f_i$ is the fraction of tokens dispatched to expert $i$; $P_i$ is the average router probability assigned to expert $i$. This product is minimized when both quantities equal $1/N$.
Each expert has a fixed capacity: capacity = (tokens_per_batch / N) × capacity_factor. Capacity factor 1.0 means perfect balance fills every expert exactly; >1.0 leaves slack for routing imbalance.

Tokens that overflow an expert's capacity are dropped — they bypass the FFN via the residual connection. Switch Transformer can train successfully even with mild token dropping; the auxiliary loss keeps it bounded.

items: Switch-Base (4× the parameters of T5-Base at the same per-token FLOPs) trains 4-7× faster to the same loss as T5-Base.
Switch-XXL demonstrates 1.6 trillion parameters trained successfully with 2048 experts.
Quality on downstream NLP tasks (SuperGLUE, SQuAD, summarization, translation) matches or exceeds the dense baselines.

blocks.html: Other findings: low precision (bfloat16) training works at scale with some routing-precision tricks; distillation back to a dense model recovers most of the sparse model's quality at a fraction of the size.

pages.title: MoE in the modern LLM stack

blocks.html: Switch Transformer was the cleanest demonstration that MoE could scale to trillions of parameters and stay trainable. The simplifications (top-1 routing, expert capacity, drop-on-overflow) became the template.

Modern MoE descendants: GLaM (Google), GShard, the Mixtral family (Mistral's open MoE), DeepSeek-MoE, the OpenAI / Anthropic models widely believed to use sparse MoE at frontier scale. MoE is now the dominant scaling strategy at the trillion-parameter frontier.
